rows.title: Vanishing bounds for Romik's sequence $v(n)$ modulo odd prime powers
rows.record_statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p\equiv3\pmod4$, let $e\ge1$, and let $(v(n))_{n\ge0}$ be the sequence defined in the paper. **The second conjecture.** If $e$ is odd, then

$$
v(n)\equiv0\pmod{p^e}
$$

for $n\ge\frac{(ep+2)(p+1)}{4}$. If $e$ is even, then

$$
v(n)\equiv0\pmod{p^e}
$$

for $n\ge\left\lceil\frac{ep^2}{4}\right\rceil$, with very few exceptions. Based on data with $n\le1500$, the listed exceptions are $(p,e)=(7,8),(7,24),(7,40),(11,36)$, whose correct lower bounds are respectively $102,298,494,1095$. The conjecture is an experimentally supported strengthening of the corresponding theorem.
rows.source: Christian Krattenthaler and Thomas W. Müller, “The congruence properties of Romik's sequence of Taylor coefficients of Jacobi's theta function θ_3”, arXiv:2304.11471 (2024).
rows.what_was_proved: The odd clause holds exactly as printed: for every prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and odd e, p^e divides v(n) for n ≥ (ep+2)(p+1)/4. For even e and n ≥ ⌈ep²/4⌉, the exceptions are classified exactly: p^e fails to divide v(n) if and only if e = (p+1)(2j+1) with 0 ≤ j < (p−1)/2 and 4n = ep² + (p+1) + 4r with 4r < p+1 and an explicit coefficient (r-th coefficient of a fixed polynomial over F_p) nonzero; at every exception v(n) misses by exactly one factor of p. The classification reproduces the source's four listed exceptions and corrected bounds, and shows the list is incomplete even within its own range (n ≤ 1500): (p,e) = (3,4) at n = 10 and (11,12) at n = 366–368. The source's own Theorem 17 is a factor of two weaker. The proof bounds the p-adic valuation of a square-root series within one factor of p, and supplies the last factor (odd e) or the exact failure set (even e) from a digit-level residue formula; the Lean proof obtains the residues mod p as coefficients of an explicit square root in characteristic p built from Frobenius. Lean defines v(n) by the source's recurrence (2.6) over ℚ, proves integrality, and checks the source's eleven printed values and its (7,8) data point.

rows.title: The general equality conjecture for $H(m,\alpha)$ and $H_2(m,\alpha)$
rows.record_statement:
Let $H(m,\alpha)$ and $H_2(m,\alpha)$ be the quantities considered in the paper, with $m\geq 3$ and $\alpha\geq 2$, and define

$$
\lambda(\alpha)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{2^{j-1}}{\alpha^{2^j}}.
$$

**General equality conjecture.**

$$
H(m,\alpha)=H_{2}(m,\alpha)\quad\text{for all }m\geq 3\text{ and }\alpha\geq 2.
$$

In particular,

$$
\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{2H(m,\alpha)}{m\alpha^m}=\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{2H_{2}(m,\alpha)}{m\alpha^m}=\lambda(\alpha).
$$

This generalizes the conjectured equality at $\alpha=2$. The paper proves matching structural and asymptotic results for $H_2(m,\alpha)$, while the equality with $H(m,\alpha)$ is left open.
rows.source: Wallace Peaslee, Attila Sali and Jun Yan, “An intermediate case of exponential multivalued forbidden matrix configuration”, arXiv:2312.11446 (2023).
rows.what_was_proved: H(m, α) = H₂(m, α) for every m ≥ 3, and in fact for every α > 1: every triple-choice multigraph is matched or beaten in weight by a 2-recursive one. The source's edge-swap lemma gives only a closed vertex pair, and its Section 6 suggests combining closed sets without carrying it out. The proof normalizes cross-block edge weights by (α^{|A|}−1)(α^{|B|}−1) to force a closed pair of blocks, then uses size-weighted cloning and the convexity of α^x to homogenize the union without losing weight, iterating from singleton blocks. Lean defines triple-choice multigraphs, the weight, 2-recursiveness (Definition 1.3) and H, H₂ as maxima over nonempty finite sets, and checks small values (H(3,2) = 4, H(4,2) = 12 by exhausting all 81 choices, H₂(5,2) = 30, H₂(6,2) = 73) and that a non-2-recursive choice exists. The 'in particular' limit follows from the equality and the source's Theorem 6.2, which Lean does not formalize.

rows.title: One-step separation conjecture for genus Tutte polynomials
rows.record_statement:
Let $g$ be a positive integer, and let $\{M_i\}$ and $\{N_i\}$ be sequences of matroids. **One-step separation conjecture.** There exist two infinite sequences of matroids $\{M_i\}$ and $\{N_i\}$ such that

$$
T^{(g)}(M_i)=T^{(g)}(N_i)
$$

and

$$
T^{(g+1)}(M_i)\neq T^{(g+1)}(N_i).
$$

This conjecture asks whether the constant controlling the genus needed to distinguish infinite families can be reduced to one. The surrounding proposition establishes separation at a genus of the form $\lceil c_1g+c_2\rceil$; the conjecture that separation occurs already at $g+1$ remains open.
rows.source: Tsuyoshi Miezaki, Manabu Oura, Tadashi Sakuma and Hidehiro Shinohara, “The Tutte polynomials of genus g”, arXiv:2402.06845 (2024).
rows.what_was_proved: For every g ≥ 1 there are matroids with equal genus-g and different genus-(g+1) Tutte polynomials, so separation happens one genus up, the optimal constant in the source's Problem 5.11 (the source's Theorem 4.22 separates at genus ⌈√2·g⌉). For g ≥ 4 the new construction uses sparse paving matroids indexed by the even versus the odd vectors of {0,1}^g: an explicit bijection of g-tuples gives the equality at genus g, and a rigidity lemma (every output slot has a private input) shows that one extra slot detects the parity, giving a coefficient that differs at genus g+1. For g = 1, 2, 3 the pairs are the source's own examples (R6/Q6 and S_4n/S'_4n at n = 3, 4), with the equality and separation proved directly. Padding both matroids with i loops gives the infinite sequences. Lean defines the genus-g Tutte polynomial over Mathlib's matroids with the source's slot variables (singletons and pairwise intersections and unions), and proves the statement for every g with no hypothesis and nothing cited from the source.

rows.title: Solid $k$-minor essentiality conjecture
rows.record_statement: Let a **solid $k$-minor** be a $k\times k$ minor using consecutive rows and consecutive columns, and call a minor **$k$-essential** if it is necessary in a $k$-positivity test in the sense developed in the paper. **Solid-minor essentiality conjecture.** Solid $k$-minors are $k$-essential. The conjecture is motivated by the preceding construction of $k$-positivity tests and the observed prevalence of solid $k$-minors; proving it would identify a distinguished class of minors that every such test must include.
rows.source: Anna Brosowsky, Sunita Chepuri and Alex Mason, “Parametrizations of k-Nonnegative Matrices: Cluster Algebras and k-Positivity Tests”, arXiv:1712.05037 (2021).
rows.what_was_proved: For every n, every 1 ≤ k ≤ n and every solid position, there is an n×n matrix (rational for rational t) whose distinguished solid k-minor is 0 while every other minor of order at most k is positive, so every k-positivity test made only of minors must contain all solid k-minors. The source proved k ≤ 3 with ε-power constructions around a 0/1 central block and noted that its method fails beyond k = 3. The new construction perturbs a weighted rank-(k−1) polynomial moment kernel by two opposite rank-one terms built from a discrete binomial spline with exactly one zero divided difference; with two opposite perturbations the leading term of every other minor is a sum of two nonnegative quantities, at least one positive (one perturbation provably fails). Lean states minors over sorted index sets and k-essential as in the source, and proves the statement for every n, k and position by a general argument (a function-sum expansion in place of Cauchy–Binet, which the pinned Mathlib lacks; Lagrange divided differences; a continuity argument for the common parameter).

rows.title: The integer-scaling criterion for C-realizability
rows.record_statement:
Let $\{\frac{\lambda_1}{\alpha_1},\ldots,\frac{\lambda_n}{\alpha_n}\}$ be a multiset of rational numbers, and let $p=\operatorname{lcm}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$. Here $C_{\mathbb{Q},3}$-realizability and $C_{\mathbb{Z},3}$-realizability refer to the corresponding realizability criteria for the Nonnegative Inverse Eigenvalue Problem.

**Integer-scaling criterion.** If $\{\frac{\lambda_1}{\alpha_1},\ldots,\frac{\lambda_n}{\alpha_n}\}$ is $C_{\mathbb{Q},3}$-realizable, then it is $C_{\mathbb{Q},3}$-realizable if and only if

$$
\left\{p\cdot\frac{\lambda_1}{\alpha_1},\ldots,p\cdot\frac{\lambda_n}{\alpha_n}\right\}
$$

is $C_{\mathbb{Z},3}$-realizable.

This criterion would remove the dependence on the particular sequence of realizability rules used to establish $C_{\mathbb{Q},3}$-realizability, reducing the question to an integer-scaled multiset whose scaling factor depends only on the denominators of the entries. The supplied text does not establish the equivalence, so its resolution is unclear.
rows.source: Alberto Borobia and Roberto Canogar, “A simplification of the C-realizability criterion for the Nonnegative Inverse Eigenvalue Problem for integers”, arXiv:2401.07857 (2024).
rows.what_was_proved: A rational multiset is C_{Q,3}-realizable exactly when its p-scaled integer multiset (p the least common multiple of the denominators) is C_{Z,3}-realizable; in fact every rational C3 derivation can be replaced by an integer one at scale p, and conversely. The C3 rules are those of the source's Theorem 7 and Definition 9: start from {0}, join two realizable multisets, raise the Perron root, or transfer a positive amount from the Perron root's partner to a nonpositive entry. The proof normalizes a derivation so that a leader absorbs finished blocks one at a time while an outstanding debt is passed up, and then shows that every step can be chosen as an integer in a closed-form region (the leaders are fixed by their terminal values and losing leaders are frozen), which is the integer-rounding statement no prior paper gives. Lean defines C3 inductively over an ordered ring, proves the unconditional direction rational-to-integer and its converse, and checks that C3 over ℤ holds for {1, −1} and fails for {−1}.

rows.title: Kapranov–Schechtman's total-positivity conjecture for finite Coxeter groups
rows.record_statement:
Let $(W,S)$ be a finite Coxeter group of rank $|S|=n$. For subsets $I,J\subset S$, let $W_I$ and $W_J$ be the parabolic subgroups of $W$ of types $I$ and $J$, respectively. Define the metamatrix $M(W)=(M_{pq})_{0\leq p,q\leq n}$ by

$$
M_{pq}=\sum_{I,J\subset S,|I|=p,|J|=q}|W_I\backslash W/W_J|.
$$

**Kapranov–Schechtman's conjecture.** The metamatrix $M(W)$ is totally positive.

This extends the known type-$A$ result, where $W=S_n$, to arbitrary finite real reflection groups. The conjecture is proved in the source for type $B$ and the exceptional types, while the general finite-Coxeter-group case remains open.
rows.source: Zhentao Wang, Jiawen Xie and Xuhang Zhang, “On the Total Positivity of Contingency Metamatrices”, arXiv:2503.02213 (2025).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture fails for the Coxeter group of type D_27: the 16×16 submatrix of M(D_27) with rows p = 0..15 and columns q = 12..27 has negative determinant (a 372-digit integer), so M(D_27) is not totally positive, not even totally nonnegative. The source proves the conjecture for type B and the exceptional types and does no type-D computation; every rank from 2 to 26 is totally positive (reproduced independently by two lanes, not formalized and not claimed), so no small-rank check finds the failure. The proof identifies parabolic subgroups with stabilizers of face vectors, counts double cosets by Burnside's lemma through fixed-face counts with a type-D gluing identity (Stembridge's fixed-face data are the closest prior work), and turns the result into an explicit integer formula for every entry. Lean works with the concrete group of even signed permutations of 27 coordinates and its 27 standard reflections (the D_27 fork), defines parabolics as generated subgroups and entries as Nat.card of Mathlib's double-coset quotient, proves the formula, evaluates all 256 entries of the minor in the kernel (decide +kernel, no native_decide), and certifies the sign of the determinant by an integer triangular factorization.

rows.title: The complexity bound conjecture for S(e,23,e)-adic languages
rows.record_statement:
Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an $S(e,23,e)$-adic language, and let $p_\mathcal{L}(n)$ denote its factor-complexity function.

**Complexity bound conjecture.** The complexity function $p_\mathcal{L}$ for any $S(e,23,e)$-adic language $\mathcal{L}$ satisfies

$$
p_\mathcal{L}(n) \leq 3n.
$$

This would extend the paper's classification of TRIP maps whose associated $S$-adic languages have complexity bounded above by $3n$ to the remaining map family $S(e,23,e)$ and its twins and conjugates.
rows.source: Thomas Garrity and Otto Vaughn Osterman, “On the Factor Complexity Associated with a Family of Multidimensional Continued Fraction Algorithms”, arXiv:2410.02032 (2026).
rows.what_was_proved: For every directive sequence over the two substitutions of the TRIP-map family S(e,23,e), the factor complexity of the S-adic language satisfies p(n) ≤ 3n for every n ≥ 1; the bound is attained. The source proves the analogous bound for the family (e,e,e), outlines the method for (e,23,e) in its Section 10 with Propositions 69–71 stated without proof, and names the remaining work: characterize the bispecial words and control their lengths. The proof does this: every double-Gauss block is a 3-free word followed by a single 3, which gives unique parsing and the exact extension sets in both directions (the source's Proposition 71, here proved); the bispecial factors are classified into 23 types; and a new cross-age matching between bispecials of different levels controls their total extension count. Lean defines the two substitutions, the directive applied with d(0) outermost as the source's Definition 14 requires, the language as the factor closure of all images, and the complexity as the number of factors of length n, and proves the bound for every directive sequence, including degenerate ones such as the all-S1 sequence.

rows.title: The Rail Conjecture for knight's tours
rows.record_statement: Let an $n \times n$ knight's tour be a closed knight's tour on an $n \times n$ board, and let a **rail** be the structure defined by the preceding discussion: a pair of edges that can be switched with their complementary pair while preserving vertex degrees. **Rail Conjecture.** An $n \times n$ knight's tour has $\Omega(n)$ rails. This conjecture is motivated by the authors' observation that all knight's tours they examined had many rails; its resolution would clarify the abundance of local switching operations in closed knight's tours.
rows.source: Ian Parberry, “Tourneys and the Fast Generation and Obfuscation of Closed Knight's Tours”, arXiv:2001.06044 (2020).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture is false: for every t ≥ 0 the (60+8t)×(60+8t) board has a closed knight's tour with no rails at all. The first refutation, by a GPT-6.1 Sol lane, was a periodic family on boards of side 252+24t with exactly 104 rails, which reduces connectivity to a fixed cycle; a Claude Opus 5.5 review cleared it. The Lean lane (Claude Opus 5.5) certified a stronger construction instead: a periodic template found by a SAT search gives a single 60×60 rail-free tour, and an induction that inserts one 8-column or 8-row period preserves the Hamiltonian cycle and the absence of rails, using two local conditions checked on the reference board. Lean defines the knight graph, the tour as a Hamiltonian cycle (Mathlib's Walk.IsHamiltonianCycle), a rail literally as in the source's Section 4 (an unordered pair of tour edges (v0,v1), (v2,v3) such that (v0,v2) and (v1,v3) are knight moves not in the tour, without a 'parallel' condition, which only enlarges the rail set and so makes zero rails the stronger statement), and the conjecture as ∃ c > 0, ∃ N, ∀ n ≥ N, every closed tour has at least c·n rails; it proves the negation. The SAT output is only data checked in Lean.

rows.title: Conjecture on great-circle thrackleable trees and augmented caterpillars
rows.record_statement: A **great-circle thrackleable tree** is a tree admitting a thrackle drawing on the sphere in which the edges are great-circle arcs. An **augmented caterpillar** is the graph class defined in the source. **Conjecture on great-circle thrackleable trees and augmented caterpillars.** The class of great-circle thrackleable trees is properly contained in the class of augmented caterpillars. The conjecture is proposed as a further restriction on the class of trees that can be great-circle thrackleable; the source leaves it open and notes that crossing orientations may be relevant to proving or disproving it.
rows.source: Karen Collins and Cleo Roberts, “Great-circle Tree Thrackles”, arXiv:2110.09679 (2021).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds: every great-circle thrackleable tree (with at least three vertices) is an augmented caterpillar, and the containment is proper. The open half is strictness. The 14-vertex tree T formed by an edge 01 with three pendant 2-paths at each of 0 and 1 is an augmented caterpillar under every reading of the source's Definition 3.1 (its legs are disjoint paths), but it has no great-circle thrackle drawing in general position. The proof (GPT-6.1 Sol) encodes a drawing by the signs of 3×3 determinants of the vertex vectors (a rank-3 chirotope), imposes the 3-term Grassmann–Plücker relations and an exact table saying when a short or long great-circle arc meets another exactly once, and refutes the resulting 162,578-clause formula with an LRAT certificate; the containment half (the source's Theorem 3.2) is re-proved the same way from a certificate that the 3,3,3 spider is undrawable. Lean defines drawings on the unit sphere of ℝ³ in general position, short and long arcs, the thrackle condition (every two distinct edges meet in exactly one point) and the source's Definition 3.1 with legs, generates the input clauses by a Lean function of the tree, proves that every geometric drawing satisfies all of them, and checks both certificates by `decide +kernel` through a reflective RUP checker proved sound in Lean (no native_decide, no bv_decide, no ofReduceBool). T is the tree the source's own Conjecture 3.5 predicts is undrawable; that conjecture is neither used nor proved.

rows.title: Generalized reflectional periodicity conjecture for odd Inverse k-cross games
rows.record_statement:
Let $k=2m+1$ with $m\geq1$, and consider an Inverse $k$-cross game with empty-board state $[a]$. Let $\mathcal{G}([a])$ denote its Sprague–Grundy value, and let $\oplus$ denote nim-sum. **Generalized reflectional periodicity conjecture.** For every such game, $\mathcal{G}([a])\leq1$, and

$$
\mathcal{G}([2+3m+a])=\mathcal{G}([a])\oplus(m\bmod2),
$$

$$
\mathcal{G}([2+5m-a])=\mathcal{G}([a])\oplus(m\bmod2).
$$

For $k=2$, eventual periodicity is known through the identification with Dawson's Kayles, whereas for even $k>2$ eventual periodicity is unknown; the asserted uniform bound and reflectional periodicity for odd constraints remain conjectural.
rows.source: Kai Liang and Muxi Li, “A Weak Solution of Inverse Treblecross”, arXiv:2604.16759 (2026).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds, and more is true: for every odd k = 2m+1 the Sprague–Grundy value of the empty board of length n is (n + [n mod (3m+2) ≥ k]) mod 2. With P = 3m+2, either player can force the game to end with exactly 2⌊n/P⌋ + [n mod P ≥ k] empty cells, even when one extra nim-heap of size one is added: the board is cut into blocks of k + (m+1) cells, each containing m+1 disjoint supports and only m high cells, and the defender answers inside the block the opponent just played in. So the length of the game is fixed and its parity gives the value; the bound G ≤ 1 and both identities follow from the formula. Lean defines the game on the sets of unmarked cells (a position is legal when every window of k cells contains an unmarked cell), the options and the Sprague–Grundy value as a minimum excluded value, proves the three statements of the conjecture and the closed formula for every m ≥ 0, and proves that the moves of this model are, move for move, the placements of the source's game on a Boolean board.
